entries.justification: The contract is the allocation-and-copy cost of `Clone` on owned data like `String` and `Vec` versus passing `&str`/`&[T]`, the borrow-instead-of-clone advice that the Rust Performance Book collects; the Clippy `redundant_clone` and `clone_on_copy` lints appear only as a detection aid.

Avoiding intermediate `collect()` calls to cut heap allocations and extra passes is the allocation-and-iteration advice The Rust Performance Book collects, with the laziness of `Iterator` adapters as the underlying std behaviour.

The contract — reserve panicking accessors for bugs and invariants while recoverable I/O, parsing, and lookup failures return `Result` — is community practice built on the documented fact that `expect` panics; no single upstream document states this split.

Replacing repeated `format!` with `write!` into a reused `String` buffer to avoid per-iteration heap allocations is exactly the kind of allocation-reduction guidance The Rust Performance Book gathers, and the rule frames it as a measured hot-path decision.

The rule's own text concedes that neither indexed nor iterator syntax guarantees bounds-check elimination or vectorization, leaving the contract as an idiomatic-expressiveness argument (traversal and pairing stated directly, less hand-written index/length coordination) rather than a documented language, std, or lint guarantee.

The rule derives from Tokio's documented distinction between `std::sync::Mutex` and `tokio::sync::Mutex` — that a synchronous guard held across `.await` can block or deadlock a runtime worker while an async guard serializes waiting tasks — with Clippy's `await_holding_lock` cited only as enforcement.

The rule states and configures Clippy's `ptr_arg` lint, which is precisely the policy that a `&String` parameter should be `&str`; the deref-coercion explanation is supporting mechanism rather than the source of the contract.

Beyond the documented fact that `Option::unwrap` and `Result::unwrap` panic, the rule's actual contract — that input, dependency, configuration, and shutdown failures must become typed errors rather than panics, with `expect` reserved for proved invariants — is general service-engineering practice rather than a single upstream document.
Same origin as the `&String` rule: Clippy's `ptr_arg` lint, named in the rule, is what makes `&Vec<T>` parameters a reportable defect where `&[T]` works.

This applies the API Guidelines' builder-pattern guidance together with its convention of flagging returned values that are useless when discarded, so a chained `-> Self` builder method cannot be silently dropped; Clippy's `return_self_not_must_use` and `must_use_candidate` are listed only as enforcement.

The contract is the standard library's own convention for consuming fallible methods — String::from_utf8 returns the bytes inside FromUtf8Error, BufWriter::into_inner returns the writer inside IntoInnerError, and Rc::try_unwrap returns the original Rc — so a recoverable failure does not destroy an irreplaceable receiver.

The rule's whole argument is the standard library's documented blanket impl `impl<T, U> Into<U> for T where U: From<T>` in `core::convert`, which is why implementing `From` is sufficient and implementing `Into` directly is not; Clippy's `from_over_into` lint only enforces that std contract.

Same API Guidelines source as the AsRef rule — take `impl Into<T>` to loosen parameter assumptions (C-GENERIC) and implement `From` rather than `Into` as the conversion-trait convention (C-CONV-TRAITS).

This is the API Guidelines' newtype guidance — wrapping primitives in distinct types so semantically different values such as `UserId` and `GroupId` cannot be interchanged — extended with the guidelines' advice on eagerly deriving common traits on those wrappers.

The rule text itself invokes the Rust API Guidelines' position on operator overloading (C-OVERLOAD): implement `std::ops` traits only where the meaning is unsurprising, plus the guidelines' related advice to implement arithmetic for reference operands.

The sealed-trait pattern, a public trait with a private supertrait in a hidden module so downstream crates can call but not implement it and methods can be added without a breaking change, is the API Guidelines' sealed-trait guidance verbatim in structure.

The rule rests on the documented contract of the standard library's `AsyncFn`, `AsyncFnMut`, and `AsyncFnOnce` traits in `std::ops` — that they mirror `Fn`/`FnMut`/`FnOnce` receiver semantics and tie the returned future's borrow to the call, unlike a hand-written `F: Fn() -> Fut, Fut: Future` pair.

The contract is Tokio's `tokio::sync::mpsc` API: `channel(capacity)` makes `send` await when the buffer is full while `unbounded_channel` never applies backpressure, plus the documented `try_send` `TrySendError::Full`/`Closed` cases and `reserve` permits.

The whole contract is tokio::sync::broadcast's documented behaviour — every subscriber created by Sender::subscribe receives every message, messages must be Clone, and a slow receiver observes RecvError::Lagged rather than backpressure.

This is Tokio's documented cancellation-safety contract — `select!` drops the futures of branches that did not complete, and Tokio marks which primitives such as `mpsc::Receiver::recv` and `AsyncReadExt::read` are cancel-safe versus `read_exact`/`read_to_end`, which lose partially accumulated state.

The rule is built entirely on `tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken` and its documented API — `cancelled()`, `cancel()`, `is_cancelled()`, `child_token()`, `drop_guard()` — together with Tokio's contract that dropping a `JoinHandle` detaches rather than cancels the task.

The rule hangs on tokio::spawn's documented bound that a spawned future must be Send + 'static (with spawn_local/LocalSet as the non-Send alternative), which is what forces an Arc::clone rather than a borrow; the Send/Sync properties of Arc and Rc it leans on are std contracts.

This is language semantics: an async fn in a trait desugars to an opaque associated future that carries no Send promise, and the dyn-compatibility rules exclude such methods from trait objects; the trait-variant and async-trait crates appear only as workarounds.

Built on the documented semantics of tokio's join! and try_join! macros — branches polled in one task rather than spawned, try_join! returning the first error and dropping the remaining branch futures, plus the biased poll option and futures' buffered/buffer_unordered for dynamic fan-out.

Every claim is a tokio::task::JoinSet contract: spawn/join_next yielding results as they complete, JoinError distinguishing panic from cancellation, abort_all, and aborting remaining tasks when the set is dropped.

Derives from tokio::sync::mpsc's API contract — async send/recv with bounded capacity for backpressure, cheap Sender clones, the channel closing when all senders drop, Sender::downgrade/WeakSender, and reserve() permits — contrasted against std::sync::mpsc's blocking recv.

States tokio::sync::oneshot's contract: a single-use channel consumed by await, RecvError when the sender drops, send returning the value back when the receiver is gone, and is_closed/closed for detecting an abandoned receiver.

Documents tokio::select! behaviour — racing branches with pattern bindings and if guards, dropping losing futures at their next await point, the random-by-default versus biased; poll order, and the else branch when all branches are disabled — with futures::future::select_all for dynamic sets.

The contract is `tokio::fs`'s documented behaviour of delegating blocking regular-file syscalls to Tokio's blocking pool, so awaiting it frees a worker without making the syscall asynchronous or cancellable, which is what forces the explicit byte, file-count, and concurrency bounds the rule prescribes.

Turns on tokio's try_join! contract — concurrent polling of a fixed tuple in one task, return on the first observed error, and dropping unfinished branch futures without any rollback — plus futures' try_join_all/buffered for the dynamic case.

Describes tokio::sync::watch's contract: receivers see only the most recent value, changed() plus borrow()/borrow_and_update(), send_if_modified for change-gated notification, and the Ref guard that must not be held across an await.

The rule is built on the 2021 edition's disjoint closure capture change (RFC 2229), where closures capture individual fields rather than whole variables — a behaviour change the Edition Guide documents as an edition migration.
The `FnOnce`/`FnMut`/`Fn` hierarchy, which closures implement which trait, and the cited bounds on `Iterator::map` and `thread::spawn` are documented contracts of standard-library traits and APIs.

The contract rests on language semantics — each closure has a distinct unnameable type that `impl Trait` in return position preserves but cannot unify across branches, while `Box<dyn Fn>` erases it behind a vtable; the allocation/dispatch cost framing also touches performance-book territory.

The rule states language semantics the compiler enforces: the `move` keyword makes a closure capture its environment by value rather than by reference, which is what lets the closure satisfy the `'static` bound required to escape its defining scope, and `move` is orthogonal to which of `Fn`/`FnMut`/`FnOnce` the closure implements.

Choosing monomorphized `impl Fn` against `&dyn Fn`/`Box<dyn Fn>` on grounds of code size, storage of heterogeneous closures, and measured hot paths is an engineering trade-off with no single upstream document stating it.

The contract is the documented behaviour of `std::collections::BinaryHeap`: it is a max-heap whose `pop` removes the greatest element and `peek` returns it without removing, with `std::cmp::Reverse` inverting the ordering to obtain a min-heap, and no arbitrary removal or priority-update operation offered — stated without attributing the rule's O(log n) figures to std.

The selection criteria mirror the `std::collections` module documentation's guidance on when to use `HashMap` versus `BTreeMap`, including `BTreeMap::range` and the note that the default hasher is randomized and its algorithm unspecified; `IndexMap` is the one non-std option named.

`Vec` as the default sequence, `VecDeque`'s amortized O(1) push/pop at both ends, the O(n) cost of `Vec::remove(0)`, and the standard library's own discouragement of `LinkedList` all come from the `std::collections` documentation.

The O(n) cost of `Vec::contains` against expected O(1) `HashSet` membership, `BTreeSet`'s sorted iteration, and `Vec::dedup` requiring adjacent equal elements are documented standard-library complexity contracts.

The Relaxed/Acquire/Release/AcqRel/SeqCst taxonomy and the release-store to acquire-load happens-before argument are the documented contract of std::sync::atomic::Ordering; the loom section is supporting tooling, and the same material is also covered by the Nomicon's atomics discussion.

Entirely rayon's contract — rayon::prelude, par_iter/par_iter_mut and the parallel reduce, par_sort_unstable_by, with_min_len/with_max_len granularity control, and the work-stealing scheduler's Send/Sync requirements plus its unsuitability for blocking I/O.

States the documented guarantees of std::thread::scope: the Scope handle lets spawned threads borrow non-'static data from 'env, every scoped thread is joined before scope returns, and a child panic is re-raised by the scope.

The rule describes the language semantics of inline `const { }` block expressions — forced compile-time evaluation, use as an expression in array initializers and function bodies, and how they differ from a named const item.

The contract is what `const fn` means to the compiler — callable in const contexts such as array lengths, const and static initializers, and const-generic arguments, with the set of const-evaluable operations growing per release — plus a secondary API-compatibility note about removing `const`.

Const generic parameters are language semantics — a `const N: usize` parameter is part of the type, each value monomorphizes separately so types with different values are non-interchangeable, and permitted parameter types are limited to integers, `bool`, and `char` — with no stabilization release asserted here.

The rule rests on std::convert::AsMut's documented contract as the mutable counterpart of AsRef and on which std types lend `&mut [u8]` (Vec, arrays, slices), making one generic parameter accept all of them; the API-shape framing parallels the API Guidelines' generic-parameter advice.

The contract is std::str::FromStr's documented relationship with str::parse — implementing the trait with its Err associated type is what makes `.parse::<T>()` and `T: FromStr` bounds work — with clap's value_parser noted only as a downstream consumer.

The rule is entirely about `Cargo.toml` package manifest fields — `description`, `license`, `repository`, `keywords`, `categories`, `readme`, `rust-version`, `include`/`exclude` — and the `cargo package`/`cargo publish --dry-run` verification flow, which are Cargo manifest and publishing behaviour.

No single upstream document prescribes unifying README and crate root docs; the rule combines the `#[doc = ...]` attribute with `include_str!` and the Cargo `readme` field into a single-source-of-truth practice, with the doctest-tagging advice being ordinary rustdoc hygiene.

The `# Errors` documentation section for fallible functions is the API Guidelines documentation convention for `Result`-returning APIs (the failure/documentation checklist items), with Clippy's `missing_errors_doc` cited only as enforcement.

The policy of showing only the meaningful lines of an example rests on the API Guidelines' documentation expectations for examples, while the '# ' hidden-line mechanism itself is a rustdoc feature; because the class list has no rustdoc entry the attribution is a judgement call.

The requirement that prose link to the types and methods it names is the Rust API Guidelines documentation item on hyperlinking, with rustdoc's intra-doc link syntax and the broken_intra_doc_links lint as the mechanism.
Documenting panic conditions in a '# Panics' section is the Rust API Guidelines documentation item requiring error, panic, and safety considerations on function docs.
Using `?` rather than unwrap in rustdoc examples is a named Rust API Guidelines documentation item about how examples should handle errors.

The obligations the rule requires a '# Safety' section to enumerate — validity invariants, alignment, initialization, provenance, aliasing, ownership transfer, and unwinding across FFI — are the soundness obligations the Rustonomicon defines; the section convention itself also appears in the API Guidelines and is checked by clippy::missing_safety_doc, so the class is a judgement between them.

The contract is Cargo's `[lints.rust]` table carrying `unexpected_cfgs` with `check-cfg` entries, Cargo automatically registering declared `feature` names, and workspace lint inheritance via `[workspace.lints]` / `[lints] workspace = true`; the rustc lint itself is only the mechanism the manifest configures.

The rule exists because the `clippy::nursery` lint group exists and names individual nursery lints (`significant_drop_tightening`, `redundant_clone`, `use_self`, `redundant_else`, `or_fun_call`) whose behaviour and unstable status come from Clippy's own lint documentation.

The rule exists because the `missing_docs` lint exists and simply states a policy for it (warn then deny, `pub`-only scope, `#[allow]` overrides, `[lints.rust]`/workspace configuration); note this is a rustc lint rather than a Clippy one, so the lint-policy class is an approximate fit.

The whole rule is policy over the `clippy::pedantic` lint group and named members of it such as `doc_markdown`, `semicolon_if_nothing_returned`, `wildcard_imports`, `module_name_repetitions`, and `must_use_candidate`.

The rule is built on the Clippy lints `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, and `missing_safety_doc`, and states the enforcement level and override policy for them, even though the proofs it demands are soundness reasoning.

The contract is the language's macro-export semantics — `#[macro_export]` placing a macro at the crate root and path-based macro import replacing `#[macro_use] extern crate` — documented in the Rust Reference's macros-by-example and macro-scoping material; the 2018-edition framing means edition-guide is a plausible alternative.
The fragment-specifier table and the follow-set restriction on what tokens may appear after `:expr`, `:ty`, and `:pat` are defined by the Rust Reference's Macros By Example chapter.

The contract belongs to the `syn` crate's error API — `syn::Error::new`, `Error::new_spanned`, `Error::combine`, and `to_compile_error` — together with `quote` and `proc-macro2` for emitting the resulting token stream.

Both halves — `macro_rules!` hygiene for locally introduced identifiers and `$crate` expanding to the defining crate rather than the caller's — are language semantics specified in the Rust Reference's Macros By Example chapter.

The rule is the `arrayvec` crate's contract: `ArrayVec<T, N>` and `ArrayString<N>` store elements inline with fixed compile-time capacity, `push` panics when full while `try_push` returns a `CapacityError`.

The rule rests on Rust's type-layout rules: the default representation gives no stable size or field order across compilers, targets, and features, while `repr(C)` and `repr(transparent)` define representation contracts and niche optimization can change size.

This is the allocation-avoidance advice the Performance Book collects under heap allocations and string handling — do not build an owned `String` for constant text, and prefer borrowed or `Cow` returns on hot paths.

The underlying fact is the language's enum layout semantics — an enum value must be able to hold its largest variant, so boxing that variant's payload shrinks every instance — and Clippy's `large_enum_variant` merely reports the condition rather than creating the contract.

It derives from `Clone::clone_from`'s documented contract — the default implementation is `*self = source.clone()`, and concrete impls such as `String`/`Vec`/`PathBuf` may instead reuse existing capacity.
The contract belongs to the `compact_str`, `smartstring`, and `ecow` crates, whose inline and shared string representations (and their version-specific inline capacities) the rule is entirely about.

The rule states the language's destructor semantics — struct fields and tuple/array elements drop in declaration order, locals in reverse declaration order, temporaries at end of statement — which is defined by the language rather than by any library contract.

This is type-size and layout advice of the kind that book collects — shrinking struct footprint by choosing narrower integer and float fields, padding and field-ordering effects under `repr(C)`, bitflag packing, and `NonZero` niche use for `Option`.
The rule is the `smallvec` crate's contract (`SmallVec<[T; N]>` stores up to N elements inline and spills to the heap beyond that), with `tinyvec` and `arrayvec` named as the alternatives.
The contract is the documented behaviour of `std::mem::take` (replaces with `T::default()` and returns the original, requiring `T: Default`), `std::mem::replace`, and the related `Option::take`.
The contract belongs to the `thin-vec` crate: `ThinVec<T>` keeps length and capacity behind the pointer so the handle is one word, trading indirection for a smaller inline field.

The contract is that `format!` constructs an owned `String` while `write!`/`writeln!` render into an existing target through `std::fmt::Write` or `std::io::Write`, returning a `Result` those traits define.

The contract is the allocation-avoidance advice that book collects — sharing payload bytes through borrowed slices, `Cow`, and refcounted buffers such as `bytes::Bytes` instead of copying into owned `String`/`Vec` — with the crate references (bytes, memchr) serving as illustrations rather than the source of the rule.

The casing convention that acronyms are treated as one word (HttpServer, not HTTPServer) is the Rust API Guidelines' naming/casing item, itself codifying RFC 430, and the rule's evidence is std names like TcpStream and UdpSocket.

SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for consts and statics is the casing convention in the Rust API Guidelines naming chapter (RFC 430), separately enforced by rustc's non_upper_case_globals lint that the rule mentions as compiler warnings.

The advice against `-rs`/`-rust` crate-name suffixes is a crates.io community naming habit the rule illustrates with real crate names (serde, tokio, reqwest, clap), not a contract stated in the API Guidelines checklist or any other single upstream document.

snake_case for functions, methods, variables, and modules is the value-level casing convention in the Rust API Guidelines naming chapter (RFC 430), backed by rustc's non_snake_case lint the rule quotes.

The into_ prefix for self-consuming conversions comes from the Rust API Guidelines conversion-naming item, illustrated here with String::into_bytes, Vec::into_boxed_slice, and IntoIterator::into_iter.

The is_/has_/can_/should_ prefix table is general naming practice generalized from std predicates (Option::is_some, str::is_ascii, Path::is_file) rather than from a specific API Guidelines checklist item I can name, so I mark it low-confidence as an attribution.

Short lifetime names ('a, 'b, 'src, 'ctx) are community convention with no single upstream document I can cite; the one concrete borrowing is serde's 'de from its Deserialize trait, so confidence in any stronger attribution is low.
The to_ prefix marking a conversion that allocates or computes is the Rust API Guidelines conversion-naming item, shown here with to_string, to_vec, to_lowercase, and the ToOwned trait.

It restates the API Guidelines naming convention that generic parameters are concise single uppercase letters with conventional meanings (`T`, `E`, `K`, `V`), matching the std signatures the guidelines point to.

The casing convention for types, traits, and type aliases (`UpperCamelCase`, acronyms treated as words) is the API Guidelines naming checklist item, which rustc's `non_camel_case_types` lint enforces.
Enum variants fall under the same API Guidelines casing convention as types (`UpperCamelCase`), again backed by the `non_camel_case_types` warning quoted in the rule.

The rule's core justification is the language semantics of the `as` cast operator — silent truncation on narrowing integer casts and saturating float-to-integer conversion with `NaN` mapping to zero — with std's `From`/`TryFrom` offered as the safe alternative; it is arguably std-docs instead, since the losslessness convention is a standard-library contract.

The contract comes from documented `f32`/`f64` behaviour — `PartialOrd::partial_cmp` returning `None` for NaN, `total_cmp`'s IEEE totalOrder-compatible ordering, `is_nan`/`is_finite`, and `to_bits` — rather than from Clippy's `float_cmp` lint, which the rule never mentions.

The rule is organized around the standard library's `checked_*`/`saturating_*`/`wrapping_*`/`overflowing_*` method families and their documented return types, with the debug-panic vs release-wrap default as supporting context.

Every claim is a documented standard-library contract: `Ord::clamp` panicking when `min > max`, `f32`/`f64::clamp` propagating `NaN` from the value and panicking on a `NaN` bound, and the `saturating_*` integer methods stopping at the type's limits.

This is bounds-check-elimination advice of the kind that book collects — prefer iterator, `windows`, `chunks_exact`, and `split_at` traversal over indexing in hot loops, and verify generated code before reaching for unchecked access; the guaranteed-panic-on-out-of-bounds premise itself is language semantics, so the source is mixed.

The rule is about the Cargo profile key `codegen-units`, named profiles with `inherits`, differing defaults per profile, and the documented fact that a library's own profile settings are ignored when it is built as a dependency.

The contract is the `#[cold]` codegen attribute as the language documents it — a hint that a function is unlikely to be called, carrying no guarantee of section placement, branch weighting, or inlining behaviour.
It derives from the documented semantics of the `#[inline(always)]` attribute as a stronger code-generation hint that the compiler may still decline, not a language guarantee.
The rule combines the documented `#[inline(never)]` and `#[cold]` attributes, both defined as code-generation hints rather than promises about machine-code placement.

The contract is the `#[inline]` attribute family's documented status as codegen hints, together with the language's cross-crate inlining model in which a non-generic body may be unavailable downstream without the attribute or LTO.

The contract — representative and versioned training workloads, pinned `llvm-profdata` matching the toolchain, holdout validation, and promoting only the measured artifact — is a build-pipeline discipline assembled by the author around rustc's `-Cprofile-generate`/`-Cprofile-use` flags rather than a policy any one of the listed documents states.

The rule is organized around standard-library SIMD surfaces — nightly `std::simd` with `slice::as_simd`, `std::arch` intrinsics, `is_x86_feature_detected!`, and the `#[target_feature]` safety obligation — with the `wide` crate shown only as a stable alternative.

The rule derives from the allocation- and copy-avoidance guidance that book collects (do not clone a `String` or owned graph merely to read it), with the caveat that `Arc` clones are refcount bumps and cloning is right when independent ownership is needed.
It derives from the documented split between `std::clone::Clone` (explicit `.clone()`, may be expensive, has a `clone_from` hook that can reuse storage) and `Copy`'s implicit duplication.

The rule restates the documented requirements and semantics of `std::marker::Copy` — every field `Copy`, no `Drop`, implicit duplication on move — plus the list of standard `Copy` types including `&T` but not `&mut T`.
The whole rule is the documented contract of `std::borrow::Cow`: hold `Borrowed` or `Owned`, clone only via `to_mut`/`into_owned` when mutation or ownership is required.
The three elision rules, the `'_` anonymous lifetime, and where elision fails are language semantics specified in the Rust Reference's lifetime-elision rules.

General engineering advice — borrow by default, box only for recursion, address stability, stack limits, or a measured copy — with no single upstream document behind it, though the recursive-type case is a language requirement.

It derives from `std::sync::Mutex`'s documented contract: guard-based exclusive access, `Send`/`Sync` conditioned on `T: Send`, lock poisoning surfaced as a `Result` with `into_inner`, and no promised fairness or implementation.
The contract is `std::rc::Rc`'s documented non-atomic reference counting, its `!Send`/`!Sync` status, and the documented leak-on-cycle behaviour that `Weak`/`downgrade`/`upgrade` exist to break.

It derives from `std::cell::RefCell`'s documented runtime borrow tracking — `borrow`/`borrow_mut` panic on conflict while `try_borrow`/`try_borrow_mut` return `BorrowError`/`BorrowMutError` — and from `Cell`'s get/set alternative.

The rule rests on `std::sync::RwLock`'s documented semantics: many readers or one writer, poisoning, and an explicitly unspecified/platform-dependent fairness policy that makes writer starvation possible.

This is the API Guidelines' flexibility guidance that public functions should minimize assumptions about their parameters (the `&[T]`/`&str`/`&Path` parameter idiom); Clippy's `ptr_arg` lint enforces the same shape, so the classification is arguable.
The `name @ pattern` binding syntax and the positions in which patterns may appear are language grammar and semantics from the Rust Reference's Patterns chapter.

The rule's prerequisite is the 2024 edition, since let chains are gated on it, which is what the Edition Guide covers; the Reference documents the syntax itself, so rust-reference is a defensible alternative.
`let ... else` and its requirement that the else block diverge are language semantics specified in the Rust Reference's statement and pattern material, not an edition-gated or lint-driven contract.

Every claim restates the documented contract of `std::hint::black_box` — a best-effort optimization barrier with no guarantee about inlining or timing — stabilized in the standard library and used here from Criterion benchmarks.

The rule's core claim — that `Iterator::chain` costs a branch per item under `next()`-driven consumption and should be restructured in hot loops — is measurement-driven iteration advice rather than a documented std guarantee; std documents that `Chain` exists and overrides some internal-iteration methods, but not the per-item branch cost the rule reasons from.

The contract is the book's collection-reuse advice — clear and refill a buffer via `Extend`/`extend` so the existing capacity is reused instead of allocating a fresh collection per loop iteration — with `Iterator::collect_into` noted as the still-unstable spelling.

The contract is the documented capacity behaviour of `Vec::drain`, `Vec::clear`, `HashMap::drain`, and `mem::take` — removal without releasing the allocation, versus `take` resetting capacity to zero.

It derives from the documented behaviour of the `Extend` trait and `Vec::extend`/`extend_from_slice`/`append`, specifically that reservation depends on the iterator's `size_hint` and is therefore not a guaranteed single allocation.

It rests on documented `std::io` contracts: `BufReader`/`BufWriter` batch operations on the inner handle, `BufRead` supplies `lines`/`read_line`/`read_until`, buffer capacity is an unspecified implementation detail, and dropping a `BufWriter` discards errors from the final write so `flush` must be called explicitly.

It restates the standard library's documented iterator contract that adaptors are lazy and do nothing until consumed, and enumerates which `Iterator` methods are adaptors versus consumers such as `collect`, `any`, and `find`.

The rule explicitly disclaims any performance guarantee and argues instead from source-level contract clarity (off-by-one ranges, silent length truncation, index/value drift), an engineering argument the author assembles himself; it overlaps Clippy's `needless_range_loop` policy but the rule does not derive from that lint.

The contract is Cargo's target auto-discovery convention documented in the Cargo Book — files under src/bin/ (and src/bin/<name>/main.rs) become binary targets without [[bin]] sections, plus the manifest keys the rule shows (path, required-features, default-run) and the --bin/--bins selection flags.

The rule derives from the language's visibility and privacy semantics as specified in the Rust Reference: pub(super) makes an item visible in the parent module and everything nested within it, sitting between private, pub(in path), pub(crate), and pub.
The contract is serde's `#[serde(default)]` and `#[serde(default = "path")]` field and container attributes, including that they affect deserialization only and require `Default` at container level.

The four representations and their limits are serde's own container-attribute contract — the default externally tagged form, #[serde(tag = "...")], #[serde(tag, content)], and #[serde(untagged)] — including serde's documented restriction that internally tagged enums cannot carry tuple or primitive-newtype variants.

It derives from serde's `#[serde(flatten)]` attribute, including its documented incompatibility with `deny_unknown_fields`, its content-buffering deserialization path, and its unsuitability for non-self-describing formats such as bincode.
The rule states serde's `rename_all` container attribute, the exact set of case values it accepts, and the precedence of a field-level `rename` over it.

Built on serde's `skip_serializing_if`, `skip`, `skip_serializing`, and `skip_deserializing` attributes and their documented predicate signature and `Default` requirement, with the wire-contract judgment layered on top as the crate's own guidance does not make that call.

Everything the rule prescribes is mockall's API contract: #[automock]/MockX::new, expect_* builders with with/withf and mockall::predicate matchers, times counts, Sequence ordering, returning closures, and expectation verification on drop.

The contract is the built-in `#[should_panic]` testing attribute, its `expected =` substring matching, and the compiler rule that such a test must return `()`, all of which are language/test-harness behaviour described in the Reference's testing attributes.

The workflow and assertions belong to the insta crate — assert_debug_snapshot!/assert_json_snapshot!/assert_snapshot!, .snap and .snap.new files, cargo insta review, and the INSTA_UPDATE environment control used to fail CI on unapproved snapshots.

The contract is language semantics of trait declarations: an associated type is bound once per implementation while a generic trait parameter admits several implementations of the same trait for one type (as with `Add<Vec2>` and `Add<f64>` for the same struct), and that difference is what drives the guidance regardless of the rule file's own nod to the API Guidelines.

The load-bearing content is language-level coherence: a blanket impl is permitted because the trait is local, and it cannot overlap a specific impl because specialization is unstable (error E0119); the semver caveat is a secondary Cargo-book concern and the ToString-for-Display example is std.

The design advice — keep a minimal orthogonal required set and build defaults on top, overriding only for performance — is generalized from how std::iter::Iterator, std::io::Read, and std::io::Write are written rather than from a stated guideline, and the file's attribution to the API Guidelines' 'implement common traits from std' item does not actually cover default methods.

The rule restates the Rust Reference's dyn-compatibility (object-safety) rules — which methods are vtable-dispatchable, the exclusion of generic methods, by-value Self returns and associated constants, and the where Self: Sized escape hatch — with E0038 as the compiler's enforcement.

The rule restates the API Guidelines checklist item C-DEREF — implement Deref/DerefMut only for smart-pointer and transparent wrapper types, not as inheritance — and the file names that item directly.

Bound minimization, moving bounds from structs to impls, and preferring where clauses for readability is general Rust engineering style rather than a contract stated in any single upstream document, though it overlaps the API Guidelines' advice to minimize assumptions about generic parameters.

The contract is language semantics for the never type `!` — divergent function return types, coercion of `!` to any type, and which uses are stable versus still feature-gated — with std::process::exit and std::convert::Infallible as illustrations.

The rule is the API Guidelines checklist item C-NUM-FMT, that numeric types should support the LowerHex, UpperHex, Octal, and Binary formatting traits wherever the underlying primitive does; the file names that item.

The contract comes from std::option::Option's documented role as the type for an optional value plus its combinator API (map, and_then, ok_or, as_ref/as_deref, `?` on Option) that the examples exercise.

The contract is std::marker::PhantomData's documented behaviour — a zero-sized marker that makes an otherwise unused type parameter legal and tells the compiler the type acts as if it owned or borrowed a T — with the variance and drop-ownership discussion overlapping the Nomicon's PhantomData material, so the split between the two is not clean.

The factual basis is the documented behaviour of standard-library string APIs — str::len returns the length in UTF-8 bytes while chars() yields Unicode scalar values, and std offers no grapheme-cluster segmentation — though the surrounding policy of naming and enforcing one unit at every boundary is the rule's own engineering advice, so the attribution is only partial.

The contract is the Rustonomicon's soundness reasoning about unsafe: an unsafe fn states a caller obligation rather than blessing its whole body, each unsafe operation needs a local proof of its preconditions, and safe code must not be folded into the trusted surface; the unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn and Clippy undocumented_unsafe_blocks lints are cited only as enforcement.

This is the Rustonomicon's treatment of Send and Sync as unsafe auto traits — that Send permits cross-thread ownership transfer and Sync (equivalently &T: Send) permits shared cross-thread access, so a wrong manual unsafe impl lets safe code cause data races — together with the ownership, aliasing, destructor, and interior-mutability obligations a manual impl must discharge.
